messages.subject: Dump Data Format
parts:
Hi,

I'm very new to stan, and only just have started exploring it. It looks very promising. One thing that makes me uncomfortable though is the data dump format. 

What is the reasoning behind the S-like custom syntax to specify a basic data structure? This seems to make it unnecessarily hard to call stan from a non-S-like environment, like javascript or julia. Perhaps consider adding support for a more general purpose data interchange format like JSON?

Below some examples from the manual, as they could be represented in JSON. Excellent JSON parsers and writers are available for both R and C++.


5.1. Scalar Variables

{ 
  "y" : 17.2 
}

5.2. Sequence Variables

{
  "n" : [1,2,3],
  "y" : [2,0, 3.0, 9.7]
}

{ 
  "n" : {"type" : "seq", "from" : 1, "to" : 2 } 
}

5.3. Array Variables

{ 
  "y" : {"type" : "structure", "data" : [1,2,3,4,5,6], "dim" : [2,2] } 
}

or:

{ 
  "y" : [ [1,2], [3,4], [5,6] ]
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dump Data Format
parts:
JSON's a good idea for an I/O format.

The motivation for the S-like structure is
that it was easy for us to generate the output and
it's what we already had data for in all the models
we wanted to test in JAGS.

At least it was supposed to be easy, but R's dump
output is rather idiosyncratic (the format varies
by content, so the output format for array { 1, 2, 3 }
is different than that for { 1, 2, 4}.

Presumably JSON could deal with ragged arrays, which
would also be very useful.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: JSON data/sample format & Python interface
parts:
There's a boost lib that parses JSON into a
DOM-like property tree:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_53_0/doc/html/property_tree.html

We'd just need to implement our data interface on top of
a property tree the same way we have done for reading
from files and reading from the R environment.

I'm less clear on JSON output -- I don't see anything
to write JSON-formatted data, though it's bound to
be a lot easier than parsing if we need to write it
ourselves. The output needs to come in the form of
headers and then lines of data, and will hopefully be
streamable.

We might literally be able to set a compiled Stan
model up to work as a pipe taking JSON-formatted
data as standard input and producing JSON-formatted
data as standard output with control given by the
command-line options of the compiled Stan model. With
that, a fully-functional, basic Python interface should
be really simple.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] JSON data/sample format & Python interface
parts:
We'd implement JSON I/O completely independently of Python.

That'd certainly make it easier to call in the unix pipe style
from Python or other languages. But I think the original poster's
suggestion was that it'd just be easier to write the necessary
Stan input files and parse Stan output files if they were in
a standard format like JSON instead of the quirky dump format that
R inherited from S.

There are advantages to a simple pipe-like interface --- it
requires far less maintenance and documentation. The RStan
interface wraps a dynamic lib (which is a DLL on Windows) at
the memory level rather than going through files. But that
means whenever the command-line interface changes (for instance
we add a new sampler type as we just did for 1.2), the Python
program has to change.

Python looks like it'll let us do a deeper API-style integration
if we wanted, rather than just implementing the command. So
we might wrap up our current samplers (implemented as iterators)
in Python iterators.

I think most users would probably like the command, though, implemented
either as a pipe to one or more external processes or through memory/dynamic
linking.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] JSON data/sample format & Python interface
parts:
While JSON offers certain advantages for data exchange, it would also pose a significant barrier to entry for some potential users.  For example, I do most of my data manipulation and analysis in Stata. While the R-dump format is, uhm, different, it is brutally straight-forward.  Writing code to write my data into the R-dump format was pretty straight-forward and didn't require me to know anything about R.    Writing out my data in JSON, however, would be significantly more difficult and require me to learn about the intricacies of a moderately convoluted data format (at least relative to R-dump).  

At the moment, I suspect most users to Stan are already users of Python or R, meaning they have easily available tools for producing a JSON file and probably the programming expertise to make it a non-issue.  If the hope is to grow the use of Stan towards a slightly more general audience, however, JSON might be sub-optimal.  Since the Stan syntax itself is pretty straight-forward for someone comfortable with the statistical concepts, just getting the data ready to go might actually be the biggest barrier for some.

An old-fashioned comma (or tab) delimited file with variable names in the top row (data.csv) may have disadvantages in this setting that I don't grasp, but I would offer it for consideration as (a) very easy to produce from almost any package, (b) not connected to any particular statistical package (the term "r-dump file" is infelicitous to the ear of someone who hasn't used R), and (c) easy to import into almost any package, even if it is subsequently munged into something else.  Since Stan output is comma-delimited, it also provides a nice symmetry.

Just something for your consideration.  I'm enjoying learning to use Stan and find it a powerful, useful package.  Thanks to all who are moving it forward!

Glenn Hoetker

Arizona State University

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] JSON data/sample format & Python interface
parts:
I haven't been using Stan as much as I could, but Jeroen's remark makes me think that you're overanalyzing this.  Many users won't ever use Stan directly.  If you want someone to use a stats tool, it should probably resemble Excel, the most widely used statistical analysis package in the known universe.   The data can live in a table, but the relationships that define pivot tables, functions, etc. are substantially more complicated, and it's those we're concerned about.

As long as your data structures are flat (like tables), a CSV file is great.  The instant your data structures diverge from a regular tabular structure, something like JSON has enormous advantages in terms of representing hierarchies, etc. in an easily parsed form, supported by a vast number of potential "producer" and "consumer" applications.  If Stan is going to take over the world it might as well support distributed operation, which is greatly facilitated by having this sort of widely supported data exchange format.  

Here's one scenario to consider.  You have smallish samples (relative to the complexity of the model you want to fit) and a lot of semi-technical people with domain knowledge and common sense, but no real interest in programming.  They just want to know where to buy ads, what stuff to work on, etc.  They notice that Bayesian models tend to offer better predictive performance in such situations and would like to build and fit them without learning how to program.  They're willing to consider pictures of distributions, etc. and have a program generate pictures of marginals, posteriors, etc. for sanity checking, and they'd like to store the models that did / did not work somewhere "in the cloud" (i.e., somewhere they don't have to back up manually, like Dropbox or a database).  Some clever guy realizes that he can be a hero if he rigs up a web interface that guides people towards less-stupid model choices and draws some pictures for them to sign off on when each model is constructed.  Then the models get shipped off to Stan, which grinds through them as compute power permits, and the users get emails when their models converge, along with a reference to allow predictive fits on new data that looks like the old data. 

Maybe users drag and drop colorful bits into a canvas object or some such (I'm already throwing up a little bit in the back of my mouth).  It would sure be nice to compactly represent those distributions and their relationships to each other, wouldn't it? Especially if you wanted to visualize certain marginal or posterior distributions.  But if everything is in a CSV-formatted table with a fixed number of columns, you have to somehow kludge in a place for any dependencies between variables.  With a loosely structured "object" (list of stuff) like JSON or YAML allows, you just pass everything & pull it back out on the other end. 

Something like this: http://www.jsoneditoronline.org/  (See?  Not so complex!)

The rules are simple: Lists in { curlies }, arrays in [ brackets ], separate different items with commas.  If there's anything more brutally simple, I haven't seen it. 

JSON became a de facto standard because it's just about the simplest thing that could possibly work, for the task.  People would just use CSV if it were easier, but for passing around data structures, it rapidly becomes apparent that it's actually harder with a flat tabular representation.  Strange but true.

Anyways, that's my piece for the day.  YMMV and I respect your opinion.  But I disagree with it, and I wanted to lay out my reasoning for why I disagreed.

Best,

--t

parts:
This isn't an either-or situation. We can implement multiple
data formats and let users use whatever they like. The only
thing holding us back is programming time. So if someone wants
to volunteer to write a JSON interface, we can help you plug
it into Stan's C++ layer. JSON's pretty easy, but unfortunately,
like R's dump format, doesn't have a built-in typing mechanism
for integer vs. real values.

The way Stan actually works is that it has a low-level
abstract base class representation for reading data that gets
called in the constructor of a class that reads data and then
is used to evaluate log probabilities and gradients and transforms.

Currently the abstract base class is implemented three different ways:

- reading from R-style dump format streams/files (used in CmdStan)

- reading from R data structures/environments (used in RStan)

- reading from Python data structures (not sure the details, used in PyStan)

Writing something to read from a std::ostream for JSON is on
our to-do list, but not a high priority at the moment. If someone wants
to take it on, we're happy to help!

Andrew's asked for something to read from CSV files, but given his
response (most of our data's non-rectangular), we've apparently been
succesfull in explaining why it's challenging.

We haven't thought much about bringing something like Stan down
to users who don't know stats --- the whole thing's based on writing
your own probability function! Our target's more the people who understand
how to express the log probabilty function for their model, but don't want
to code a sampler/estimator for it.

We have thought about GUIs and cluster distribution to make exploring
models easier. But nothing's come of it because we don't have
any GUI programmers and we only have half-formulated ideas on how to
make it work in limited domains like hierarchical GLMs. Andrew and Ben
have gone down this path with their multiple imputation (mi) package in R,
so maybe they have some insight to offer.

We have thought about shipping models off to the cluster to grind
through --- in fact, we're doing that. But model fitting is usually more
of an interactive process where you don't try twenty models at once, but
you try one, see how it works and what you learn from fitting it, and
then use that to guide the next model. Just managing all the results
and model specifications is hard in this setting, which is why it would
be nice to automate it with a GUI or scripting language or something.

- Bob

I've thought about writing the reader for JSON, but I've been stuck for a while because there aren't standard conventions in JSON.

Tim points out:

Thanks for the recap. I'm not sure how to deal with the intricacies of "curlies" and "brackets." Here's a quick example that I can figure out:

Stan model:
  data {
    int N;
    real x[N];
  }

An example piece of JSON data:
  {
    "N": 3,
    "x": [
      0.1,
      0.2,
      0.3
    ]
  }

For this example, I think it's straightforward, but what happens if x is reported as a list? Or as brackets in brackets? Like [ [0.1], [0.2], [0.3] ].

Here's a more complex example. Suppose the data block looks like:
  data {
    int I;
    int J;
    int K;
    real a[I];
    vector[I] b;
    matrix[I,J] c;
    real d[I,J,K];
  }

This isn't an either-or situation.  We can implement multiple
data formats and let users use whatever they like.  The only
thing holding us back is programming time.  So if someone wants
to volunteer to write a JSON interface, we can help you plug
it into Stan's C++ layer.  JSON's pretty easy, but unfortunately,
like R's dump format, doesn't have a built-in typing mechanism
for integer vs. real values.

The way Stan actually works is that it has a low-level
abstract base class representation for reading data that gets
called in the constructor of a class that reads data and then
is used to evaluate log probabilities and gradients and transforms.

Currently the abstract base class is implemented three different ways:

   - reading from R-style dump format streams/files (used in CmdStan)

   - reading from R data structures/environments (used in RStan)

   - reading from Python data structures (not sure the details, used in PyStan)

Writing something to read from a std::ostream for JSON is on
our to-do list, but not a high priority at the moment.  If someone wants
to take it on, we're happy to help!

Andrew's asked for something to read from CSV files, but given his
response (most of our data's non-rectangular), we've apparently been
succesfull in explaining why it's challenging.

We haven't thought much about bringing something like Stan down

your own probability function!  Our target's more the people who understand
how to express the log probabilty function for their model, but don't want
to code a sampler/estimator for it.

We have thought about GUIs and cluster distribution to make exploring
models easier.  But nothing's come of it because we don't have
any GUI programmers and we only have half-formulated ideas on how to
make it work in limited domains like hierarchical GLMs.   Andrew and Ben
have gone down this path with their multiple imputation (mi) package in R,
so maybe they have some insight to offer.

We have thought about shipping models off to the cluster to grind
through --- in fact, we're doing that.  But model fitting is usually more
of an interactive process where you don't try twenty models at once, but
you try one, see how it works and what you learn from fitting it, and
then use that to guide the next model.  Just managing all the results
and model specifications is hard in this setting, which is why it would
be nice to automate it with a GUI or scripting language or something.

- Bob


On 12/18/13, 1:38 PM, Tim Triche, Jr. wrote:

I haven't been using Stan as much as I could, but Jeroen's remark makes me think that you're overanalyzing this.  Many

most widely used statistical analysis package in the known universe.   The data can live in a table, but the
relationships that define pivot tables, functions, etc. are substantially more complicated, and it's those we're
concerned about.

As long as your data structures are flat (like tables), a CSV file is great.  The instant your data structures diverge
from a regular tabular structure, something like JSON has enormous advantages in terms of representing hierarchies, etc.
in an easily parsed form, supported by a vast number of potential "producer" and "consumer" applications.  If Stan is
going to take over the world it might as well support distributed operation, which is greatly facilitated by having this
sort of widely supported data exchange format.

and a lot of semi-technical people with domain knowledge and common sense, but no real interest in programming.  They
just want to know where to buy ads, what stuff to work on, etc.  They notice that Bayesian models tend to offer better
predictive performance in such situations and would like to build and fit them without learning how to program.  They're
willing to consider pictures of distributions, etc. and have a program generate pictures of marginals, posteriors, etc.
for sanity checking, and they'd like to store the models that did / did not work somewhere "in the cloud" (i.e.,

fits on new data that looks like the old data.

back of my mouth).  It would sure be nice to compactly represent those distributions and their relationships to each
other, wouldn't it? Especially if you wanted to visualize certain marginal or posterior distributions.  But if
everything is in a CSV-formatted table with a fixed number of columns, you have to somehow kludge in a place for any
dependencies between variables.  With a loosely structured "object" (list of stuff) like JSON or YAML allows, you just
pass everything & pull it back out on the other end.

Something like this: http://www.jsoneditoronline.org/  (See?  Not so complex!)

The rules are simple: Lists in { curlies }, arrays in [ brackets ], separate different items with commas.  If there's
anything more brutally simple, I haven't seen it.

JSON became a de facto standard because it's just about the simplest thing that could possibly work, for the task.
  People would just use CSV if it were easier, but for passing around data structures, it rapidly becomes apparent that
it's actually harder with a flat tabular representation.  Strange but true.

Anyways, that's my piece for the day.  YMMV and I respect your opinion.  But I disagree with it, and I wanted to lay out
my reasoning for why I disagreed.

Best,

--t

What got me thinking about this is a grant that I wrote a while ago that revolves around dynamic model averaging as a means to model structural changes in 20-30 years' worth of pre- and post-op survival probabilities in a disease where there have been a lot of structural changes.  Writing the grant got me thinking about how best to structure the backend (i.e. minimal intervention required from the users) but also make the assumptions/features considered by the model fit apparent to users.  In other words, both the model fitting and model checking need to be transparent (check!), and should be intuitive (more challenging). 

Say you have a drug that didn't exist prior to 2001 and a segment of the population that responds, if not beautifully, at least a lot better when treated with it.  Now say you have a dozen such drugs punctuating the history of the disease, along with some of the most meticulous record keeping in medicine.  It would be very nice for clinicians NOT to try and extrapolate from disparate data sets what is/is not informative, since the data and its temporal relationship to various innovations is capable of telling you more, but rather use estimates from a collection of models where structural NAs are marginalized out.  Since the model predictions and marginal estimates could be very consequential, this has to be as transparent as possible to the target group of domain experts, and it ought to be possible to re-run the fit accordingly, subject to certain privacy protections on the original data (which is obviously valuable).  

I ran this by the domain experts in question, who were generally thrilled about not trying to draw statistical conclusions from disparate, previously published point estimates.  And obviously since they're the experts (pulling the trigger, when it comes right down to it) they need complete transparency as well.

This sort of thing (albeit with, IMHO, less transparency) has worked fine for other diseases with single structural innovations.  It's a bit of a paradox that it doesn't exist for the disease and procedure in question, but hopefully the above paragraph illustrates some pitfalls and potential remedies available by making the process transparent to domain (not statistical) experts.  I knocked together a prototype frontend in a couple hours a long time ago, thanks in part to the enormous number of libraries available in R.  However, for a lightweight frontend that eats spreadsheets, it would be more scalable to have it in JavaScript, with the best collection of models, their weights, and the new data run through a comparatively trivial pipeline to give instantaneous estimates.  Even a computation of credible intervals should not be too much for client code to manage.  Full re-fits of the data, for many reasons (privacy, DoS worries) more or less have to be done somewhere else, but the user ought to have the option to pick a refitted model if necessary (e.g. another structural innovation) and push it back to the origin if it outperforms the existing ones.

As I was thinking about this, it dawned on me that simply shipping things around as JSON was probably the easiest way to represent these things, and if I'm going to write something like that for the grant, I might as well write it for Stan (minimal marginal effort).  So (contingent upon funding), I plan to do so.

On Wed, Dec 18, 2013 at 12:30 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

This isn't an either-or situation.  We can implement multiple
data formats and let users use whatever they like.  The only
thing holding us back is programming time.  So if someone wants
to volunteer to write a JSON interface, we can help you plug
it into Stan's C++ layer.  JSON's pretty easy, but unfortunately,
like R's dump format, doesn't have a built-in typing mechanism
for integer vs. real values.

The way Stan actually works is that it has a low-level
abstract base class representation for reading data that gets
called in the constructor of a class that reads data and then
is used to evaluate log probabilities and gradients and transforms.

Currently the abstract base class is implemented three different ways:

   - reading from R-style dump format streams/files (used in CmdStan)

   - reading from R data structures/environments (used in RStan)

   - reading from Python data structures (not sure the details, used in PyStan)

Writing something to read from a std::ostream for JSON is on
our to-do list, but not a high priority at the moment.  If someone wants
to take it on, we're happy to help!

Andrew's asked for something to read from CSV files, but given his
response (most of our data's non-rectangular), we've apparently been
succesfull in explaining why it's challenging.

We haven't thought much about bringing something like Stan down
to users who don't know stats --- the whole thing's based on writing
your own probability function!  Our target's more the people who understand
how to express the log probabilty function for their model, but don't want
to code a sampler/estimator for it.

We have thought about GUIs and cluster distribution to make exploring
models easier.  But nothing's come of it because we don't have
any GUI programmers and we only have half-formulated ideas on how to
make it work in limited domains like hierarchical GLMs.   Andrew and Ben
have gone down this path with their multiple imputation (mi) package in R,
so maybe they have some insight to offer.

We have thought about shipping models off to the cluster to grind
through --- in fact, we're doing that.  But model fitting is usually more
of an interactive process where you don't try twenty models at once, but
you try one, see how it works and what you learn from fitting it, and
then use that to guide the next model.  Just managing all the results
and model specifications is hard in this setting, which is why it would
be nice to automate it with a GUI or scripting language or something.

- Bob


On 12/18/13, 1:38 PM, Tim Triche, Jr. wrote:

I haven't been using Stan as much as I could, but Jeroen's remark makes me think that you're overanalyzing this.  Many
users won't ever use Stan directly.  If you want someone to use a stats tool, it should probably resemble Excel, the
most widely used statistical analysis package in the known universe.   The data can live in a table, but the
relationships that define pivot tables, functions, etc. are substantially more complicated, and it's those we're
concerned about.

As long as your data structures are flat (like tables), a CSV file is great.  The instant your data structures diverge
from a regular tabular structure, something like JSON has enormous advantages in terms of representing hierarchies, etc.
in an easily parsed form, supported by a vast number of potential "producer" and "consumer" applications.  If Stan is
going to take over the world it might as well support distributed operation, which is greatly facilitated by having this
sort of widely supported data exchange format.

Here's one scenario to consider.  You have smallish samples (relative to the complexity of the model you want to fit)
and a lot of semi-technical people with domain knowledge and common sense, but no real interest in programming.  They
just want to know where to buy ads, what stuff to work on, etc.  They notice that Bayesian models tend to offer better
predictive performance in such situations and would like to build and fit them without learning how to program.  They're
willing to consider pictures of distributions, etc. and have a program generate pictures of marginals, posteriors, etc.
for sanity checking, and they'd like to store the models that did / did not work somewhere "in the cloud" (i.e.,
somewhere they don't have to back up manually, like Dropbox or a database).  Some clever guy realizes that he can be a
hero if he rigs up a web interface that guides people towards less-stupid model choices and draws some pictures for them
to sign off on when each model is constructed.  Then the models get shipped off to Stan, which grinds through them as
compute power permits, and the users get emails when their models converge, along with a reference to allow predictive
fits on new data that looks like the old data.

Maybe users drag and drop colorful bits into a canvas object or some such (I'm already throwing up a little bit in the
back of my mouth).  It would sure be nice to compactly represent those distributions and their relationships to each
other, wouldn't it? Especially if you wanted to visualize certain marginal or posterior distributions.  But if
everything is in a CSV-formatted table with a fixed number of columns, you have to somehow kludge in a place for any
dependencies between variables.  With a loosely structured "object" (list of stuff) like JSON or YAML allows, you just
pass everything & pull it back out on the other end.

Something like this: http://www.jsoneditoronline.org/  (See?  Not so complex!)

The rules are simple: Lists in { curlies }, arrays in [ brackets ], separate different items with commas.  If there's
anything more brutally simple, I haven't seen it.

JSON became a de facto standard because it's just about the simplest thing that could possibly work, for the task.
  People would just use CSV if it were easier, but for passing around data structures, it rapidly becomes apparent that
it's actually harder with a flat tabular representation.  Strange but true.

Anyways, that's my piece for the day.  YMMV and I respect your opinion.  But I disagree with it, and I wanted to lay out
my reasoning for why I disagreed.

Best,

--t

I'm not sure what you mean by internal vs. external here. Do
you mean internal as in the model class's constructor storing
data as member objects and external as in a file format for I/O?
In that case, internal storage is a C++ issue and I think we should
do it with natural C++ data types, not by passing streams of bytes
around in some encoding.

Having said that, if we want to think about issues like cross-chain
communication from different processes, we'll need a spec for
sending data across processes.


I think there are also several I/O interfaces we're thinking
about without being very clear about it in this thread.

1. Data input

This is already abstracted in a var_context object. All we'd
need to add JSON data input is an implementation of var_context
that accepted JSON. And of course, as Michael and Daniel mentioned,
a specification for how we code up structured objects in JSON.

We don't need to handle everyone's JSON --- we get to define our
own format here. We could base that on an R version if it's
sensible.

2. Inits input

This is also implemented in a var_context object. So whatever
works for data input should also work for inits.

3. Sample/optimization output

I know less about this one. I know Michael wrote an mcmc_writer
abstraction at some point. This would need to be implemented with
JSON. We'll need another JSON spec for how to dump output. The
output's a little more complicated because there is text, the ongoing
samples, adaptation, etc.

4. Command, etc. "pacifier" output

The command also dumps out information as it goes, like how many iterations
have been completed. We probably don't need to do this with any more
structure than a text stream. Or do we?

We need arbitrary K-dimensional arrays. So that'd be last-index
major. See the R dump format for how it's done now.

C++ array indexing and Stan's array indexing is row major
at run time.

Eigen's matrix indexing is column major by default and that's
what we went with. It's all just a huge pain to translate back
and forth, but we've done it before.

What's the motivation for converting the models to a structured
notation? To do that right, you'd need to get into our model
parser code. From what I can tell, we only need to be able to
code up arbitrary n-dimensional arrays with names.

We can do the coercion to matrices or whatever on the inside.
At least that's what we did with the R dump format. A 2D
array and matrix are represented the same way in the dump format,
then the reader pulls out the dimensions and values and converts
as necessary. Similarly, we look for scientific notation or
decimals and treat anything that has them as floating point (real),
whereas if there aren't any of those, it's a valid int (which can
be converted to real).

- Bob

parts:
Re: JSON
--------------

No, JSON does not encode types. That makes is VERY flexible, especially when combining
numerical and textual data.

JSON really just defines a format for arbitrarily nested key/value pairs. If we wanted to use
JSON then we'd have to define a spec on top of that which defines

- required keys and their valid value formats
- optional keys and their valid value formats

There is a lot of flexibly in how we define this, which I would consider a plus.

Re: Stan I/O
----------------

My opinion is that we have three layers.

Internally Stan uses C++ types.

The immediate interface to those C++ types is JSON (or another format, but only one format)
with a well-defined spec for input data/inits and output samples/optimization/configuration.

To facilitate our users we would have parsers to and from JSON to a variety of formats such
as Rdump, csv, etc. This would isolate the core of Stan from all of this I/O junk. Also we would
have a JSON to stream translator for screen output (this would also facilitate the refactoring of
command.hpp).

A writer class would handle the translation from C++ to JSON and then any additional formats.
A matching reader would do the same the other way. The mcmc_writer (perhaps an optimizer_writer, etc)
and var_context would interface with these classes.
